claims.text: High-entropy alloys can be used as intermediate layers in plasma-facing reactor components.
Current isotropic high-entropy intermediate layers provide robust mechanical strength.
Current isotropic high-entropy intermediate layers have only moderate thermal conductivity.
Plasma-facing reactor materials must tolerate high temperature, high heat flux, and intense high-energy neutron flux.
The relevant operating range for the proposed HEA intermediate layer is 600–1200°C.
Directional hot rolling or forging followed by controlled annealing can reorient the HEA into an aligned, columnar grain structure.
Directional processing can transform an Al0.3CoCrFeNi HEA from a dendritic structure to columnar crystals or even single crystals.
A textured, interconnected columnar grain network aligns higher-thermal-conductivity crystallographic directions with the principal heat-flow direction.
Grain alignment increases the continuity of high-conductivity crystallographic paths.
The aligned paths facilitate more efficient phonon and electron heat transport through the HEA.
The directional treatment maintains grain-boundary stability sufficient to preserve mechanical strength under reactor stresses.
Directional solidification increased the fracture strength of Al0.3CoCrFeNi by 80% relative to ordinary casting.
The directional thermomechanical treatment will measurably increase thermal conductivity along the heat-flux path relative to an isotropic control.
The treatment will not significantly reduce strength, fatigue life, or microstructural integrity under reactor-relevant exposure.
The predicted benefit should persist under 600–1200°C exposure, cyclic mechanical loading, and irradiation.
Excessive thermal cycling or irradiation could disrupt the aligned microstructure and eliminate the benefit.
The exact conductivity improvement and long-term microstructural stability are uncertain.
